newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks attack plan for investor code.
newsitem.headline: German banks attack plan for investor code.

text.p: A war of words is brewing between Germany's banks and the country's fledgling securities watchdog over plans to impose tougher rules on how banks treat investors.

The German Banking Association (BdB) has protested bitterly against the regulations which are designed to improve investor protection and have been detailed in a draft directive by the Federal Securities Supervision Authority (BAWe).

If implemented, the directive would force German-based banks and discount brokers to produce detailed accounts of client interviews, offer added information on products and risk and seek more data on customers than now.

In a statement sent to the BAWe last month and made available on Tuesday, the BdB said the measures were impractical, intrusive and expensive and warned that they would make Germany a less attractive place to do business.
"German banks' operational leeway would be disproportionately reduced; this would lead to a massive competitive disadvantage for Germany as a financial centre," the statement said.

The Frankfurt-based BAWe, however, is adamant that the new regulations are essential to upgrade Germany's existing securities trading laws and clarify the legal obligations of discount brokerages -- a relative novelty here.

The directive is the first the BAWe has proposed since it started operations in 1995, charged with implementing a raft of tight new securities legislation -- including a ban on insider trading -- designed to clear up Frankfurt's image.
While conceding that amendments to its proposals would be considered, the BAWe said its basic content was sound.

"These are regulations based on the EU's securities directive. We may be the pioneers in implementing them, apart from the U.K., but the rules will eventually be enforced all over Europe," spokesman Juergen Oberfrank told Reuters.

However the BdB argued that laws that work in Britain are not transferable to Germany, where the predominant system is "universal" banking, which combines retail, commercial and investment banking services under one roof.
The BdB also cast doubt on whether other European countries would implement legislation that would match the "thick layer of controls" now applying in Germany.
Moreover, the BdB said the laws would probably deter investors from working with German institutions instead of giving them a sense of improved security.
Many clients already viewed bank questions about their personal lives as an "excessive state infringement of their personal rights" and were irritated by being bombarded with product information.
As is usual practice in Germany, the BAWe will review reactions from the various bank and investor bodies affected by the directive at a closed hearing on October 23.
A final version of the directive will be prepared soon after this month's hearing and legislation will be passed "as soon as possible," Oberfrank said.
